entry: German industrialist and humanitarian. He is credited with saving about 1,200 Jews during the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] by employing them in his factories. He joined the Abwehr, Nazi Germany's military intelligence service, in 1936 and was arrested for espionage by Czechoslovakia in 1938 but released. In 1944 he moved his factory to Brünnlitz, sparing his workers from [[Auschwitz concentration camp|Auschwitz]]. He spent his fortune on bribes and [[Black market|black market]] supplies. After the war he failed in business and relied on support from the Jews he had saved. He is the subject of the 1982 novel *Schindler's Ark* and its 1993 film adaptation, *Schindler's List*.

Pair of interim agreements (1993 and 1995) between Israel and the [[Palestine Liberation Organization|Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO)]]. They created the Palestinian Authority, which was given limited self-governance over parts of the [[West Bank|West Bank]] and the [[Gaza Strip|Gaza Strip]], and led to mutual recognition between Israel and the PLO. The accords did not create a Palestinian state and deferred core issues such as borders, Jerusalem and settlements. Palestinian militant groups and Israeli far-right groups opposed them, and Israeli prime minister [[Yitzhak Rabin|Yitzhak Rabin]] was assassinated in 1995 by a right-wing extremist for signing them.

Capital and largest city of Norway (pop., 2025: 724,290), constituting both a county and a municipality. The greater urban area had 1,110,887 residents in 2025. Founded as a city in 1040 under the name Ánslo, it became a capital under Haakon V around 1300. After a fire in 1624, a new city was built near Akershus Fortress and named Christiania. It was renamed Oslo in 1925, and in 1948 it merged with the surrounding municipality of Aker, creating the modern municipality. Oslo is Norway's primate city and a center of trade, banking and shipping, with many maritime companies. It was ranked a "Beta World City" by the Globalization and World Cities Research Network in 2008.

Eponymous founder of the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman Empire]], the ruler of a small Turkoman principality in Bithynia, northern Asia Minor. No written source from his reign survives, and the Ottomans did not record his life until the fifteenth century, more than a hundred years after his death. Historians find it difficult to separate fact from myth. Later Ottoman tradition traced his ancestors to the Kayı tribe of Oghuz Turks, but many scholars regard this as a later fabrication. The principality was well placed to attack the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine Empire]], which Osman's descendants eventually conquered. The state existed until 1922, when the sultanate was abolished.

Chemical element of the platinum group, atomic number 76, symbol Os. It is a hard, brittle, bluish-white [[Transition metal|transition metal]] discovered in 1803 by Smithson Tennant, who named it for the smell of its volatile oxide, from the Greek *osmḗ*, "smell." Osmium is the densest stable element, with a density of 22.587 g/cm³ at 20 °C, slightly greater than that of iridium (22.562 g/cm³). It occurs in trace amounts, mainly alongside other platinum-group metals and in copper and nickel ores. Alloys with platinum and iridium are used in fountain pen nibs and electrical contacts because of their hardness and durability. Osmium tetroxide, which is highly toxic, is used in electron microscopy.

Net movement of solvent through a selectively permeable membrane, tending to equalize solute concentrations on the two sides. Osmotic pressure is the external pressure required to prevent this movement, and it depends on the molar concentration of the solute rather than its identity. Osmosis is a specialized form of [[Diffusion|diffusion]]. Biological membranes are semipermeable, so osmosis provides the main means by which water enters and leaves cells, and cell turgor pressure is largely maintained by osmosis across the [[Cell membrane|cell membrane]]. Water crosses membranes through aquaporin channels. Jean-Antoine Nollet first documented osmosis in 1748. Reverse osmosis uses external pressure to separate solutes from solvents, as in [[Water purification|water purification]].

[[Bird of prey|Fish-eating bird of prey]] (*Pandion haliaetus*) with a nearly worldwide range. It is a large raptor, more than 60 cm (24 in) long, with a wingspan of 180 cm (71 in). The upperparts are brown, and the head and underparts are grayish. Ospreys occur on all continents except Antarctica, and in South America only as nonbreeding migrants. They nest near water and feed almost exclusively on fish, which they catch by diving feet first. [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] described the species in 1758. It is the only living member of the family Pandionidae, and four subspecies are generally recognized. Populations declined in the mid-20th century after pesticides such as [[DDT|DDT]] thinned eggshells, and they recovered after the 1972 U.S. ban on DDT.

Diverse clade of vertebrates with endoskeletons primarily of bone, commonly called bony fishes. In a cladistic sense the group includes all [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]], among them mammals and reptiles. It contains most living fish, about 45 orders, over 435 families and 28,000 species. The group divides into the ray-finned fishes, [[Actinopterygii|Actinopterygii]], which make up most living fish, and the lobe-finned fishes, [[Sarcopterygii|Sarcopterygii]], which gave rise to all land vertebrates. The oldest known bony fish fossils are about 436 million years old, from the early [[Silurian|Silurian]] period. Early members had gas-filled foregut pouches that evolved into swim bladders in ray-finned fishes and into lungs in lobe-finned fishes.

Most common form of arthritis, a degenerative joint disease that results from breakdown of joint cartilage and underlying bone. Its main symptoms are joint pain and stiffness, which usually progress slowly over years. Only the joints are affected, not internal organs. Risk is greater in people who are overweight or have had a prior joint injury. Treatment includes exercise, weight loss, pain relief with [[Paracetamol|paracetamol]] or NSAIDs, and joint replacement if disability persists. More than 90% of hip and knee replacements are due to osteoarthritis. Long-term opioid use is not recommended.

Pseudoscientific system of [[Alternative medicine|alternative medicine]] that emphasizes physical manipulation of muscles and bones. In most countries, its practitioners, called osteopaths, are not medically trained. It differs from osteopathic medicine, a branch of the medical profession in the United States. Founded in 1874 by Andrew Taylor Still, it is based on the idea of a "myofascial continuity" linking every part of the body. Osteopathic manipulative treatment is most commonly used for back pain. Quackwatch has described parts, including craniosacral therapy, as having no therapeutic value and as quackery.

Systemic skeletal disorder marked by low bone mass and porous bone, which increases the risk of fracture. With age, bone resorption outpaces formation, so bones lose density. It is the most common reason for broken bones among the elderly, including the hip and spine. Bone loss accelerates after menopause, when [[Estrogen|estrogen]] declines. Risk factors include smoking, a sedentary lifestyle and medications such as [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]] and glucocorticosteroids. Osteoporosis is defined as a bone density 2.5 standard deviations below that of a young adult, measured by a DXA scan. Bisphosphonate medications reduce future fractures in people who have already broken bones.

Small [[Crustacean|crustacean]] of the class Ostracoda, sometimes called seed shrimp. About 33,000 species have been identified, of which about 13,000 are extant, grouped into seven valid orders. Typical size is around 1 mm (0.04 in), but sizes range from 0.2 to 32 mm (0.0079 to 1.3 in). The body is flattened from side to side and enclosed by a bivalve-like shell, or valve, made of chitin and often calcium carbonate. Ostracods are "by far the most common arthropods in the fossil record," known from the early Ordovician to the present. Because they are widespread, small and easily preserved, their valves are valuable indicators of ancient environments. Fossils from Queensland, Australia, about 100 million years old, preserved soft tissue and set a Guinness World Record for the oldest penis.

Informal name for the armored jawless fishes of the early Paleozoic era. Their gills were specialized for respiration alone, with separate pharyngeal gill pouches open along the side of the head, and they fed by using a muscular pharynx to create suction. The group is paraphyletic, and the term survives mainly as an informal umbrella term. Ostracoderms first appeared in the Ordovician–Silurian and reached their greatest diversity in the Early [[Devonian|Devonian]] period. They declined in the Middle and Late Devonian, and their last species became extinct in the end-Devonian mass extinction. Their decline coincided with the diversification of jawed vertebrates. [[Louis Agassiz|Louis Agassiz]] first studied their fossils in the 1830s, and Edward Drinker Cope named the group Ostracodermi in 1889, meaning "shell-skinned."

Large flightless bird of Africa, the heaviest and largest living bird. Two species are recognized, the common ostrich of Sub-Saharan Africa and the Somali ostrich of the Horn of Africa. Adult common ostriches weigh 63.5–145 kg (140–320 lb). They run at 70 km/h (43 mph), making them the fastest birds on land, and lay the largest eggs of any living land animal. Ostriches belong to the ratites, a group of flightless and weakly flying birds. They are farmed worldwide, with South Africa producing about 70% of global ostrich products. Ostrich leather is a lucrative commodity.

Medieval migration of ethnic Germans into Slavic, Baltic and Uralic areas of Central and Eastern Europe, and the Germanization of those areas. The term means "East settlement" in German. Larger groups of settlers, including scholars, monks, craftsmen and artisans, began moving east in the mid-12th century, often at the invitation of local princes and lords. The movement covered Germany east of the Saale and Elbe rivers, parts of Austria, [[Poland|Poland]] and the Czech Republic, and other areas of Central and Eastern Europe. It ended at the beginning of the 14th century but shaped the region's legal, cultural and economic development until the 20th century. In the 20th century, German nationalists, most notoriously the Nazis, exploited accounts of it to press territorial claims. After World War II, the movement was reversed east of the Oder River as Germans were driven out.

British fascist politician and founder of the British Union of Fascists (BUF). A Conservative MP for Harrow from 1918, he later sat as an independent, then joined the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]], serving in its 1929–1931 government. He founded the BUF in 1932 and publicly espoused antisemitism, seeking alliances with [[Benito Mussolini|Benito Mussolini]] and [[Adolf Hitler|Adolf Hitler]]. Fascist violence culminated in the Battle of Cable Street in 1936, which stopped a BUF march through London's East End. He was imprisoned in 1940, when the BUF was made illegal, and after his release in 1943 he lived mostly abroad.

Tragedy by [[William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]], written c. 1603 and set in Venice and Cyprus. The play depicts the Moorish military commander Othello as he is manipulated by his ensign, Iago, into suspecting that his wife Desdemona is unfaithful. It is usually classed among Shakespeare's major tragedies, alongside *Macbeth*, *King Lear* and *Hamlet*. Shakespeare reworked the plot from a 1565 novella by Cinthio. The play survives in one quarto edition from 1622 and in the First Folio. Originally performed by white actors in dark makeup, the role of Othello began to be played by black actors in the 19th century. Critical attention has focused on its treatment of race and on the motivations of Iago.

American soul singer and songwriter, nicknamed the "King of Soul." Born in Dawson, Georgia, he grew up in Macon and performed in local talent shows. An unscheduled appearance at a Stax Records session led to a contract and his first hit, "These Arms of Mine" (1962). Shortly before his death in a plane crash, he recorded "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay." Released in 1968, it was the first posthumous number-one on the Billboard Hot 100. His "Respect" (1965) became better known through [[Aretha Franklin|Aretha Franklin]]'s cover.

Surgical subspecialty of medicine concerned with the head and neck, also called otolaryngology or ear, nose, and throat (ENT) medicine. Its specialists, called otolaryngologists or ENT surgeons, treat conditions affecting hearing, balance, speaking, breathing, eating and swallowing. The field also manages cancers and benign tumors of the head and neck and performs reconstructive and plastic surgery of the face, scalp and neck. Subspecialties include head and neck surgical oncology, facial plastic surgery, rhinology and laryngology. In the United States, residency lasts at least five years after medical school, and total education and training typically takes 12–14 years. Laser-assisted surgery is used for tissue resection, coagulation and vaporization.

[[Capital city|Capital city]] of [[Canada|Canada]] (pop., 2021: 1,017,449), in southeastern [[Ontario|Ontario]] at the confluence of the Ottawa and Rideau rivers. It borders Gatineau, Quebec, and forms the core of the Ottawa–Gatineau census metropolitan area. It is the second-largest city in Ontario and the fourth-largest in Canada. Ottawa is the political center of Canada, home to Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Office of the Prime Minister and numerous foreign embassies. Founded in 1826 as Bytown and renamed Ottawa in 1855, it has the highest share of university-educated residents among Canadian cities. In winter the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Rideau Canal becomes the world's longest maintained ice rink.

Semiaquatic carnivorous mammal of the subfamily Lutrinae. The 14 extant species live in freshwater and marine habitats and belong to the family [[Mustelidae|Mustelidae]], which also includes weasels, badgers, mink and wolverines. Most have long, slim bodies, webbed feet and dense fur that traps air to keep them warm and buoyant. Fish is the staple of most diets, supplemented by frogs, crayfish and crabs, and sea otters use stones to break open shellfish on their bellies. Gestation lasts about 60 to 86 days, and young stay with the family for about a year. Otters can live up to 16 years. They were hunted for their pelts and feature in mythology from [[Norse mythology|Norse mythology]] to Native American totems and Asian folklore.

German chemist and pioneer of radiochemistry, called the father of nuclear chemistry. With [[Lise Meitner|Lise Meitner]], he discovered isotopes of the radioactive elements radium, thorium, protactinium and uranium. In 1938 he, Meitner, Otto Frisch and Fritz Strassmann discovered [[Nuclear fission|nuclear fission]], and Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He was an opponent of [[Nazism|Nazism]], but during World War II he worked on the German nuclear weapons program, cataloguing the fission products of uranium. Arrested by Allied forces at the end of the war, he was detained at Farm Hall with nine other German scientists. He was founding president of the Max Planck Society from 1948 to 1960 and co-founded the Federation of German Scientists in 1959.

East Frankish king (r. 936–973) and Holy Roman Emperor (r. 962–973). He was the eldest son of Henry the Fowler. Otto placed members of his family in the kingdom's most important duchies and subjected the German church to his personal control. He defeated the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955, ending Hungarian invasions of Western Europe, and conquered the Kingdom of Italy by 961. He was crowned emperor in [[Rome|Rome]] by Pope John XII in 962, following the example of [[Charlemagne|Charlemagne]]. His later years were marked by conflicts with the papacy and the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine Empire]], which he resolved through his son's marriage to the Byzantine princess Theophanu in 972. Historians regard him as a successful ruler, and his patronage fostered an "Ottonian Renaissance" of arts and architecture.

German statesman and diplomat, first chancellor of Germany (1871–1890). Known as the "Iron Chancellor," he rose in Prussian politics under King [[Wilhelm I|Wilhelm I]] and was minister president and foreign minister of Prussia from 1862 to 1890. Prussia provoked three short wars against Denmark, Austria and France. After Austria's defeat in 1866, the German Confederation was replaced by the North German Confederation, and a unified German Empire was created under Prussian rule. He created the first [[Welfare state|welfare state]] to undercut socialists and fought the Catholic Church in the Kulturkampf before allying with the Centre Party. After Wilhelm II dismissed him, he retired to write his memoirs. Historians praise him for keeping Europe peaceful for nearly two decades, but critics point to his authoritarian rule and repressive domestic policies.

Series of military conflicts between the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman Empire]] and European states from the Late Middle Ages to the early 20th century. The earliest conflicts began in Anatolia in the late 13th century and entered Europe in the mid-14th century. Ottoman expansion into the [[Balkans|Balkans]] was followed by inroads into Central Europe in the 15th and 16th centuries, reaching the peak of Ottoman territorial claims in Europe. The Ottoman–Venetian wars lasted from 1423 to 1718 and included the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571. European powers formed the Holy League and reversed many Ottoman gains in the [[Great Turkish War|Great Turkish War]] of 1683–99. Insurrections by Serbian, Greek and Romanian subjects in the nineteenth century, along with Russo-Turkish wars, weakened the empire. The final retreat began with the First Balkan War (1912–1913), and the Treaty of Sèvres after [[World War I|World War I]] led to the partitioning of the empire.
